Decompose the change of an indicator between two rounds

Source: R/decompose.R
bdhs_decompose.Rd

Splits the change of an indicator between two BDHS rounds into a composition effect (the population moved between groups, e.g. more mothers with secondary education) and a within-group (rate) effect (the indicator changed inside the groups), following Kitagawa (1955) with the symmetric weighting of Das Gupta (1993).

Usage

bdhs_decompose(
  data1,
  data2,
  indicator,
  by,
  level = 0.95,
  se = c("jackknife", "none")
)

# S3 method for class 'bdhs_decomposition'
plot(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'bdhs_decomposition'
autoplot(object, ...)

Arguments

data1, data2

Data frames of the same recode from two rounds (earlier round first).

indicator

A single indicator id (a proportion or a mean without an all-women denominator).

by

A categorical grouping variable present (or harmonizable) in both data frames.

level

Confidence level.

se

"jackknife" (default) or "none".

x, object

A bdhs_decomposition result.

...

Unused.

Value

A tibble of class bdhs_decomposition with columns component ("composition", "within", "total"), group (a group, or "All" for the sum over groups), estimate, se, ci_low, ci_high and percent (share of the total change). Proportions are on the 0-100 scale. The attribute groups holds the shares and rates by group and round; survey_1, survey_2, indicator and by describe the decomposition.

Details

With group shares \(c_{tg}\) (weighted share of the indicator's denominator population in group \(g\) in round \(t\)) and group rates \(r_{tg}\), the overall level is \(\bar r_t = \sum_g c_{tg} r_{tg}\) and $$\bar r_2 - \bar r_1 = \sum_g (c_{2g} - c_{1g}) \frac{r_{1g} + r_{2g}}{2} + \sum_g (r_{2g} - r_{1g}) \frac{c_{1g} + c_{2g}}{2},$$ the composition and within-group effects. The decomposition is exact (no interaction term), and each term is also reported by group.

Standard errors. Every term is a smooth function of weighted survey totals of the two rounds, which are independent samples, so its variance is the sum of the variances from each round. These are estimated with the delete-one-PSU jackknife within each round (the DHS Program's method for non-linear statistics such as rates): \(v_t = (k_t - 1) / k_t \sum_j (\hat\theta_{(j)} - \hat\theta)^2\) over the \(k_t\) PSUs of round \(t\), holding the other round at its full-sample value. The jackknife accounts for the clustering and the randomness of both the shares and the rates.

The groups must mean the same in both rounds: use harmonized variables (mother_edu_level, wealth_quintile, residence, division_trend6, see bdhs_harmonized_vars()). If by names a harmonized variable that is not yet in the data, it is created with bdhs_harmonize().

References

Kitagawa EM (1955). Components of a difference between two rates. Journal of the American Statistical Association 50(272): 1168-1194.

Das Gupta P (1993). Standardization and Decomposition of Rates: A User's Manual. US Bureau of the Census, Current Population Reports P23-186.

Examples

kr14 <- bdhs_simulate(2014, "KR")
kr22 <- bdhs_simulate(2022, "KR")
dec <- bdhs_decompose(kr14, kr22, "rh_del_csection", by = "residence")
dec
#> # Kitagawa decomposition: rh_del_csection by residence, BD2014DHS -> BD2022DHS
#> # A tibble: 7 × 7
#>   component   group estimate    se  ci_low ci_high percent
#>   <chr>       <chr>    <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 composition urban  0.203   4.25   -8.13    8.54   -6.11 
#> 2 composition rural -0.196   4.11   -8.25    7.86    5.90 
#> 3 composition All    0.00669 0.175  -0.336   0.350  -0.201
#> 4 within      urban -3.12    3.77  -10.5     4.26   93.9  
#> 5 within      rural -0.208   3.72   -7.51    7.09    6.27 
#> 6 within      All   -3.33    5.30  -13.7     7.06  100.   
#> 7 total       All   -3.32    5.21  -13.5     6.88  100    
attr(dec, "groups")
#> # A tibble: 2 × 7
#>   group share_1 share_2 rate_1 rate_2   n_1   n_2
#>   <chr>   <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <int> <int>
#> 1 urban    44.2    44.8   36.2   29.2    77    78
#> 2 rural    55.8    55.2   31.8   31.4    84    84
